analysis.one_liner: Caps greenhouse gas emissions through a fully auctioned cap-and-trade program, returning revenue to working families and clean energy.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to ten House committees in June 2008 with zero cosponsors, it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped U.S. greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, factories, and fuel producers starting in 2012, with the cap shrinking every year through 2050. Almost all emission permits would have been sold at quarterly auctions, with the money routed to tax credits and rebates for working families and low-income households, worker transition benefits, energy efficiency programs, clean technology development, and adaptation projects. It also would have created federal oversight of carbon markets, approved California's vehicle emissions rules, and set efficiency standards for buildings.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households gain twice: from lower long-term climate damages as the emissions cap tightens through 2050, and directly from the auction revenue — climate trust tax credits for working families and senior citizens, rebates for low-income households, weatherization and efficiency help for electricity and natural gas consumers, and income support, retraining, and health coverage tax credits for workers displaced by the energy transition [S2][S3]. Clean-energy industries gain federal research, demonstration, and deployment funding. The public also gains from a federal greenhouse gas registry that publishes who emits what [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a declining cap on greenhouse gas emissions from 2012 through 2050 — from about 6.1 billion tons down to 930 million tons of allowances — covering power plants, industrial facilities, fuel producers and importers, and natural gas distributors [S2][S3].

Auctions virtually all allowances rather than giving them free to polluters, avoiding windfall profits, with a $200-per-ton minimum penalty (or three times market value) for emitting without permits [S3].

Returns auction revenue through tax credits for working families and seniors, rebates for low-income households, and a worker transition program with income support, retraining, and health coverage tax credits for displaced workers [S2][S3].

Funds energy efficiency for electricity and gas consumers, building code upgrades, weatherization, and low-carbon technology development, plus domestic and international adaptation and forest protection [S2][S3].

Creates a FERC Office of Carbon Market Oversight to regulate carbon trading and an open, transparent quarterly auction with bidder disclosure and purchase limits, designed to prevent market manipulation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, coal-fired electric utilities, and heavy industrial emitters would buy emission allowances for every ton they emit, with costs rising as the cap tightens; some of these costs would be passed to consumers through energy prices, though the bill's rebates and tax credits are designed to offset them for lower-income households [S2][S3]. Trade-exposed manufacturers such as steel, cement, aluminum, and paper would bear compliance costs but receive free allowances covering 6 percent of the cap through 2019 to keep them competitive with foreign rivals [S3].

drawbacks.text: Cap-and-trade raises the price of fossil energy, and covered utilities and fuel providers can pass part of that cost to consumers through higher electricity, heating, and gasoline prices; the bill's compliance structure applies to power plants, industry, and fuel suppliers [S2][S3].

The trading and offset design is complex: up to 15 percent of compliance could be met with domestic offsets and 15 percent with international credits, and offset programs historically carry risks of credits that do not represent real reductions [S3].

Emission allowance prices would fluctuate with the market, creating cost uncertainty for businesses and households, which the bill addresses only partially through banking, borrowing, and penalty design [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a serious, detailed attempt to cut emissions while shielding ordinary households: it auctions permits instead of giving them away, then recycles the money to the families most exposed to energy price increases and to displaced workers. The honest trade-off is that cap-and-trade raises fossil energy prices and leans on markets and offsets that can be volatile or imperfect; a carbon tax with dividends would be simpler. But the bill's design — full auction, market oversight, per-household rebates, and a hard declining cap — addresses the standard objections more directly than most climate legislation of its era.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to ten House committees in June 2008, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the Investing in Climate Action and Protection Act on June 4, 2008 [S1][S5].

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and nine other committees, including Ways and Means, Science and Technology, Natural Resources, Agriculture, Foreign Affairs, Education and Labor, Transportation and Infrastructure, Oversight and Government Reform, and Rules [S5].
No House member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
Subsequent action was limited to additional subcommittee referrals in June 2008; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers and coal-fired utilities avoided emission costs for another two years — no cap, no auctions, and no clean-energy funding took effect. Households received no rebates, and emissions remained uncapped.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his flagship cap-and-trade proposal, predating the Waxman-Markey bill of the next Congress.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the primary referral in June 2008 and never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fossil fuel and electric utility interests
against.role: Industry groups opposing carbon caps in the 2008 climate debate
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against economy-wide carbon regulation, framing it as an energy tax, during the 2008 election season.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of potential support or opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Coal producers and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: Power plants would have needed an auctioned allowance for every ton of carbon dioxide emitted, with the cap tightening yearly through 2050, and new coal plants would face performance standards. Coal power's business model depends on emitting freely, so its interest ran against both the climate program and the cleaner energy mix it would fund.

industries.industry: Oil and gas refiners and fuel providers
industries.note: Producers and importers of petroleum- and coal-based fuels would buy allowances covering emissions from combustion of their products, and the bill adds a low-carbon fuel standard. Their revenue base is exactly what the cap prices.

industries.industry: Trade-exposed manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper)
industries.note: They would face compliance costs but receive free allowances equal to 6 percent of the cap each year from 2012 to 2019, shielding them from foreign competitors not under a carbon limit. The protection sunsets, unlike proposals that would have entrenched it permanently.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and low-carbon technology industries
industries.note: Auction proceeds fund a Low-Carbon Technology Fund for renewable research, demonstration, and deployment incentives plus carbon capture projects, and the National Energy Efficiency Fund pays for consumer efficiency, mass transit, and weatherization. Their growth depends on the very emissions reduction the public wants.

The bill creates a new multibillion-dollar allowance market that brokers and traders would profit from, but it also establishes a FERC Office of Carbon Market Oversight with registration, enforcement, and bidder-disclosure rules designed to police that market. The industry's gain is real but conditioned on transparency rules it would likely resist.
